# Page 5^page=5
Through Grief, Gaps, and Grit: My Journey from Working at 19 to the Reserve Bank of India If you are reading this after failing an exam, missing a cut-od by a fraction of a mark, or feeling like life is throwing everything it has at you please read to the end. My journey to the Reserve Bank of India was not paved with early privileges or straightforward successes. It was built on a foundation of profound grief, ﬁnancial struggle, and absolute resilience. The Early Years and The Leap of Faith I hold a Bachelor’s and a Master’s degree in Commerce. However, my professional journey started much earlier than most. To support my family, I began working at the age of 19. Over the years, I built a career from the ground up, working in management at a manufacturing unit and later in franchise management. When a friend ﬁrst introduced me to the concept of the RBI Grade B examination, the idea of serving in the apex bank took root in my mind. Driven by this new dream, I took a massive leap of faith: I quit my job to prepare wholeheartedly. A Year of Heartbreak and Margins When you quit your job to prepare, the pressure is immense. But life soon tested me in ways far beyond the syllabus. My ﬁrst reality check came when I failed my ﬁrst serious RBI Grade B attempt due to the Reasoning sectional cut-od. But the real tragedy struck later. I lost my father, and the personal devastation was unimaginable. Yet, just six days later, I gathered the courage to sit for the IBPS PO Mains exam. I missed the cut-od by a heartbreaking 0.25 marks.

# Page 6^page=6
The Day Everything Collided I pushed forward, pouring everything into my next RBI Grade B attempt, but history repeated itself. I failed the Phase 1 Reasoning cut-od again, despite clearing the aggregate. By this point, my savings had completely dried up. Desperate for a lifeline, I even applied for a QRE Content Creator role at EduTap but I wasn’t shortlisted. With no money left, I had to return to the corporate sector. The day I re entered the workforce is etched into my memory forever. On the exact same day, I secured a demanding job as an Analyst in the private sector, I lost my maternal grandmother, who had been one of my strongest pillars of support. I was grieving a massive personal loss while simultaneously trying to survive in a new corporate role. The rest of the year was brutal. Managing a full-time job of creating complex data models alongside preparation was exhausting. The hits kept coming: I missed the NABARD Grade A Mains cut-od by 0.25 marks and simultaneously failed the RBI Assistant exam. By my next attempt, I ﬁnally reached the RBI Grade B Mains but missed the interview call by 8.25 marks. It felt like I was cursed to live in the margins. But every failure was a lesson. The strategy that ﬁnally worked for me in 2025 is detailed below. The Technical Blueprint If you have read through my story above, you now understand the mindset that fueled my preparation. What follows below is the exact technical blueprint that I used to turn that mindset into a ﬁnal selection in 2025. I didn't need to study harder; I needed to study smarter. The strategies detailed in the following pages for Phase 1, Phase 2, and the Interview were born out of analyzing every single one of those past failures.

# Page 19^page=19
ESI Descriptive: I’ve outlined my general answer-writing approach later in this document, but I want to share a few speciﬁc tips for the ESI Descriptive section. First, your introduction should always open with a quote, a deﬁnition, or some background on the topic, which you then need to link directly to the demand of the question. In terms of studying, you should aim to revise your theme-based content about three to four times. On top of that, make sure to repeatedly go over the "Bingo answers" shared by the private group members on the We Learn Here channel—I personally revised those several times. When writing, my go-to ESI formula is: 80 words for the introduction. 420 words for the body (aiming for 3 positive points, 3 negative points, and 2-3 government initiatives). 100 words for the conclusion, where you absolutely must include a positive, forward-looking "way forward." Just keep in mind that this strategy won't work for every single question, so be prepared to adjust your approach when necessary. One more thing: Always quote data from the Economic Survey. It is very important.

# Page 20^page=20
Finance Descriptive: In exam this section is going dynamic and the element of surprise can’t be taken away. If you have no knowledge of Finance then complete the static portion and start answer writing on static as well as dynamic questions. Anything which is not in syllabus will not be asked. And anything which is in syllabus can be asked. I followed similar strategy for answer writing for ﬁnance descriptive and Management as well. These approaches can be followed as well: https://t.me/TargetRBI2018/24325 This is important https://t.me/TargetRBI2018/24328 Addition: You have to give real life examples of real corporate organizations to gather good marks in Management descriptive. As quoted by Irrfan Bhaiya. English: You should not use 1-9 values, (),; and others in the English paper. Use roman like I, ii, iii... etc as numbers lead to marks deductions also don’t use symbols. For writing a good essay you need to practice minimum 10-20 essays before the exam and around 5-7 essay before the mains exam (these are included in above 10-20). For important topics: Susheel sir and Brajesh Mohan sir provides a list of important essays for diderent exams you should try to write essay on those topics as they are on current topics.

I said 2-3 times that I can’t recall right now. My Final Message To the aspirant reading this: your background is not a weakness. Your gap years, your financial struggles, your current corporate job, and even your past rejections—they are building a unique perspective that no one else has. There were days I wanted to break, days when a 0.25 margin felt like a mountain, and days when the grief felt too heavy to carry. But consistency will always beat intensity. Keep showing up. Build your strategy, refine your weaknesses, and have faith that all the dots will eventually connect. Watch more about my journey on https://youtu.be/oFsQBSwRd5Y?si=rLP_Zy1-4EdiyLnh
